thread.title: The Dow Is Officially Undervalued On A Relative Basis - SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF (NYSEARCA:DIA)

author: D. H. Taylor
title: The Dow Is Officially Undervalued On A Relative Basis - SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF (NYSEARCA:DIA)
text:
Being a component of the Dow ( DIA ) has its upsides. However, there is one notable downside: When traders sell the Dow or one of its components, the counterparts companies within the Dow get drug down with it. The Dow has been selling off significantly over the past many sessions, so much so that when you look at the individual stocks within the Dow and compare them to the industry and sector, on a forward P/E basis, mostly all of them are significantly undervalued. Eventually, the stocks should move back towards their average levels, which would present a buying opportunity for these individual stocks. Y ou have to work through the numbers to uncover these opportunities.
Here is a look at the most recent Dow chart:
The general market has notably sold off from its recent highs. In fact, we are at the same level as the start of the year. Earnings for some companies have been coming in lower than expected. Some stocks have sold off significantly. The average P/E is 20.8 for the S&P 500 ( SPY ). But, when you look at the individual stocks within the Dow, they are generally below that number. There are exceptions, of course; 8 stocks are above their average number for their industry and sector.

With a few exceptions, the individual components are below the averages of their respective sector peers as well as their industry peers. There are a total of eight stocks above their respective industry peers; the rest are below.
Goldman and IBM are the two outliers that stood out for having the lowest valuations. Each are in single digits for their P/E, 8.0 and 8.8, respectively, whereas their peer group are both comfortably in double digits.
Goldman is down 27% since its peak in March and looks to continue its selling. IBM is down 24.6% since July, but, I feel that this company has an opportunity to really increase revenues with its exposure to cloud computing. So, the selling in this stock may soon fade out as future earnings are looked at a little more closely.
There are outliers to the upside, of course. Visa has a comfortable gap above its peer group. And, take a look at Walmart. Walmart has a respectable 21.9 valuation, above the S&P 500 average of 20.8. And, the company shares the same industry and sector as Amazon ( AMZN ). Of course, Amazon's P/E is significantly above the S&P 500's 20.8 P/E. However, the tech stocks are leading the selling, and Amazon is getting its fair share of down days.
I expect these overall numbers to move even more as the tech stock selling continues . Apple's stock is down 25% from its peak. The tech stock selling is seen as leading the overall market declines as valuations come more in line with fundamentals.
Why does this matter A stock that is underperforming relative to its peers generally catches up to its peers over the course of some time. Likewise, a stock that outperforms relative to its peers generally moves back in line over a period of time. Stocks tend to fall out of, or fall into, favor with investors and the push and pull has an effect on the stock on a relative basis.
You could expect 50% of stocks in this basket to be slightly above or below their peer group. But, there are only eight. Since the S&P 500 represents the most broad range of stocks from the economy, you would expect the Dow and the S&P to have some correlation. Currently, the average P/E for the S&P 500 is 20.8 , and the index has more than half of their stocks above this number.
Looking at the Dow components from this perspective, the components are undervalued relative to its peers, including the S&P 500.
That is an opportunity for an astute and creative trader. A trader could buy into the Dow from the perspective of value. But, you could also put on a hedge/pair trade.
Going Long the Dow would be profitable if the economy were going to continue to expand as it has, employment gains continuing, inflation remaining contained and interest rates remaining in line with the broader economic growth. Personally, I see these factors playing out, given the information we have today. However, the market has been selling off significantly and putting on a long trade at this time may not be for the faint of heart.
What you could do is a Long-Short pair trade. You have two choices:
Long the individual stock versus an ETF within either the industry, or sector, or Long the Dow while shorting the S&P 500, since the two are correlated. On an individual stock versus ETF basis, the size is the real issue. A very astute trader would be able to quantify the mathematics of size on this particular trade idea; the math is not simple.
However, a much easier way to trade the difference is to buy the Dow and sell the S&P, with in-kind size. Your theory would be that the markets would continue to move in correlation with each other, but, eventually the valuations would fall into line. If both indices fall, you would want the S&P to fall more, catching up to the P/E valuation of the Dow. Vice-versa, if the indices turned and moved higher, you would want the Dow component's valuations to catch up to the S&P 500.
Potential Downsides If you are going to put on a pair trade because of a disparity between to instruments, you need to understand that disparities exist and they could expand. Just ask Long Term Capital Management, who thought spreads on interest rate yields would narrow, but ultimately widened significantly and nearly brought down the world's financial markets. This proved that genius and failure are not mutually exclusive .
The spread on this trades I'm suggesting could widen, which would push the trade to a losing position.
Take Away I have put this trade on before, buying one index and selling another because of misaligned P/E ratios. It is a concept that if something is good for the goose, it is good for the gander, as well. In my opinion, the P/E ratio should generally stay in line with each other between the Dow and S&P.
With all of the selling in the general market going on, I am cautious on this trade though, as the numbers may get skewed even more.
Disclosure: I am/we are long DIA.
